passage: Call me Suraj the list-maker, Afreen. You asked how I decided, so here is the honest version. I took a page and drew a line down the middle for each offer. Pune: better projects, a team lead who writes papers, a higher package. My home city: I can stay with my parents, a friendly manager, a little less money. Twelve lines in all. And funny thing, the moment I finished I saw the list only said what I already felt: I wanted Pune. But one line surprised me. Under Pune's drawbacks I had written "deposit, first month's rent, furniture". I had not counted the cost of moving at all. It did not change my mind, but it made me ask the company what help they give with joining. That one line was worth the page.

qa.q: What did Suraj write under Pune's drawbacks?
qa.a: Suraj wrote 'deposit, first month's rent, furniture'.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when the list matched what was already felt?
qa.a: Suraj felt a quiet recognition, almost amused and reassured, because the list only said what Suraj already felt: wanting Pune.

qa.q: What alternative approach could test the wish for Pune, and why?
qa.a: Ask which choice would be regretted in two years, because a list counts items while a regret test checks the feeling behind them.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Suraj's story?
qa.a: Afreen asked how Suraj decided and gets an honest answer, so Afreen learns that the list mostly confirmed a feeling and only added one new fact.

grounding: Shows a pros-and-cons list that mainly confirmed an existing preference but revealed a forgotten cost of relocating.

passage: I was staying with Neelam's family over Diwali when she got two offers, one in Pune near home and one in Bengaluru. One night she sat at the dining table with a notebook and drew a line down the middle of two pages. Her father, Pradeep uncle, watched over his reading glasses. She wrote fast on the Bengaluru side: better name, bigger team, more learning, "exciting". The Pune side got: near home, smaller, "safe". Then she stopped and laughed. "This list is just saying what I already feel." Pradeep uncle asked, "And what would the move cost?" She frowned, then added under Bengaluru: deposit for a flat, first month's rent, travel home. She added it up on her phone and went quiet. I can't say which way she's leaning now, but the Bengaluru page had a new line circled twice.

qa.a: One in Pune near home and one in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What might Neelam have felt after adding up the moving costs?
qa.a: Neelam likely felt sobered and unsure, going quiet after the list had seemed to confirm her excitement.

qa.q: What else could Neelam do with the new cost line?
qa.a: Neelam could ask the Bengaluru company about any joining or relocation support and talk the total over with her parents before deciding.

qa.q: How does Pradeep uncle see the list?
qa.a: Pradeep uncle quietly steers her to the missing piece by asking about the cost of moving, which the list had left out.

grounding: Shows a graduate listing pros and cons of two offers, finding the list mostly mirrors existing feelings but exposes an overlooked relocation cost.

passage:
Monday. Pranav had two offers, one from a consulting firm in Gurugram and one from a mid-sized software company in his home city, Lucknow. He wrote a pros-and-cons list in his notebook. Gurugram: bigger name, faster growth, "my kind of people". Lucknow: home food, slower pace. He read it back and shrugged. It said what he already felt: Gurugram.
Wednesday. His friend Disha, who had moved to Gurugram last year, read the list on a video call. "Where's rent? The deposit? The broker's fee? Your metro card?" Pranav hadn't written a single cost. They added them up together. It came to almost two months of his first salary, before he'd even started.
Saturday. Pranav rewrote the list with a new heading, "Moving costs", and called both HR teams to ask about joining support. The Gurugram firm offered a small relocation amount. He still leaned toward Gurugram, but now with open eyes.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel reading the first list?
qa.a: Pranav felt unsurprised, even a little bored, since the list only confirmed he already leaned toward Gurugram.

qa.q: What else could Pranav add to the list now?
qa.a: He could add things like trips home for festivals and time spent commuting, so both sides show real day-to-day costs.

qa.q: How does Disha see Pranav's first list?
qa.a: Disha, who already lives in Gurugram, sees at once that it forgot the costs of moving, and helps him add them up.

grounding: Illustrates a graduate whose pros-and-cons list mostly confirms an existing lean, until a friend exposes the overlooked cost of relocating.
